title: Why Your Agent Disagrees With Itself (And What To Do About It) - Diane Lin, Datadog
talk_summary: Diane Lin (Datadog) argues that LLM agent inconsistency concentrates on decision-boundary 'gray zone' cases where the input is genuinely ambiguous, not where the model is broken. She proposes using disagreement across repeated runs as an active-learning selection signal, then resolving those cases with semantic memory (distilled policy/domain rules) and episodic memory (past similar labeled cases) instead of expensive fine-tuning.

takeaways.technique: Disagreement-based sampling instead of confidence scores
takeaways.what_they_do: Run the same input multiple times (or across models) and flag cases where verdicts differ as the high-value review set; they found LM self-reported uncertainty unreliable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the uncertainty score from LM is not very reliable... the disagreement from different runs or from different models actually give you a more reliable signal
takeaways.numbers: 93 alerts run 3x: ~25% flip-flopped without the solution

takeaways.technique: Targeted human/strong-model review of the gray zone only
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of checking every agent output, check only the subset the disagreement algorithm flags, then feed the resolution back.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You don't need to check every agent output, but instead a subset of them, which your algorithm uh active learning think is potentially problematic
takeaways.numbers: ~15% of flip-flopping cases auto-resolved by episodic memory; ~10% still needed human review

takeaways.technique: Episodic memory of past labeled cases
takeaways.what_they_do: Retrieve similar past cases and reuse their prior verdict as a reference, automating recurring decisions without distilling rules first.
takeaways.evidence_quote: identify a similar case to the one under examination and then leverage their past decision as a reference

takeaways.technique: Semantic memory of distilled policy rules
takeaways.what_they_do: When humans resolve ambiguous cases, distill the underlying policy/preference into a knowledge base so the boundary is sharpened for future runs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: human review distill the domain knowledge and put it in the semantic memory to be used next time

takeaways.what_they_do: Use several models (or the same model multiple times) and treat their disagreement as the signal for where errors concentrate.
takeaways.evidence_quote: query by committee, meaning that it by a few different models or even same model multiple times and then you identify the disagreement

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat each model disagreement as an opportunity to learn/improve rather than a bug, generating a review or rule-distillation task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the model disagreement isn't a bug, but feature. Treat each disagreement as an opportunity for your model to learn
